topics.name: Gabriel (archangel)
topics.kicker: Archangel and heavenly messenger · Honored in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
topics.briefing: In the Gospel of Luke, the angel Gabriel visits a young woman named Mary in Nazareth and tells her she will give birth to a son, Jesus, a scene Christians call the Annunciation. Gabriel is one of only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible, where he explains Daniel’s visions. Muslims know him as Jibril and believe he revealed the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad over about 23 years.
topics.answerHtml: Gabriel (or Jibril or Jibreel; accept Gavriel; do not accept “Michael” or “Raphael”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Book of Daniel, a voice commands this figure to explain a vision in which a goat with one great horn tramples a ram with two horns. This figure explains that the ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia, and the goat for the king of Greece.
tossups.r: In the New Testament, he announces the coming births of John the Baptist and Jesus. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: While Daniel was praying at the time of the evening offering, this figure came to him in swift flight and revealed a prophecy of “seventy weeks.” Along with Michael, this figure is one of only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible.
tossups.r: Muslims believe he revealed the Quran to Muhammad. For 10 points, name this archangel of the Annunciation.

tossups.p: While the priest Zechariah [“zek-uh-RYE-uh”] was burning incense in the Temple, this figure told him that his elderly wife would have a son. Because Zechariah doubted the message, this figure made him unable to speak until the baby was named.
tossups.r: That baby was John the Baptist. In the sixth month of that pregnancy, this angel visited Mary in Nazareth. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: This figure told a young woman that her elderly relative, who had long been unable to have children, was already six months pregnant, and promised that “nothing will be impossible with God.” Earlier, this figure told her not to be afraid, since she had found favor with God.
tossups.r: In the Gospel of Luke, he told Mary that she would give birth to Jesus. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: Jean-François Millet [“mee-LAY”] painted two farmers bowing their heads in a field at the sound of a church bell for the Angelus, a devotion that recalls this figure’s message. In older Catholic translations of the Bible, this figure begins that message with the greeting “Hail, full of grace.”
tossups.r: Those words open the Hail Mary. For 10 points, name this angel who announced the birth of Jesus to Mary.

tossups.p: Fra Angelico [“an-JEL-ih-koh”] and Leonardo da Vinci both painted this figure greeting a young woman, and lilies, a symbol of purity, often appear in the scene. In Simone Martini’s version, golden words of greeting stream from this figure’s mouth toward her.
tossups.r: Christians celebrate that visit, the Annunciation, on March 25. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: From 1921 until 1969, Catholics honored this figure with his own feast on March 24, the day before the feast of the event he is best known for. Since 1969, he has shared a September 29 feast, often called Michaelmas, with two other archangels.
tossups.r: Those archangels are Michael and Raphael. For 10 points, name this archangel who announced the birth of Jesus.

tossups.p: A hadith says this figure had six hundred wings when Muhammad once saw him in his true form. After this figure’s first visit, Khadija [“kah-DEE-jah”] took her husband, Muhammad, to her Christian cousin Waraqa [“WAH-ruh-kuh”], who said the visitor was the same messenger once sent to Moses.
tossups.r: Muslims believe this figure had commanded “Read!” in a cave on Mount Hira [“hih-RAH”]. For 10 points, name this angel who, Muslims believe, revealed the Quran.

tossups.p: According to Islamic tradition, this figure brought the heavenly steed Buraq [“boo-RAHK”] to carry Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem in a single night. This figure then guided Muhammad up through the seven heavens, where Muhammad met earlier prophets such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus.
tossups.r: That journey is called the Isra and Mi’raj [“mih-RAHJ”]. For 10 points, name this angel who, Muslims believe, revealed the Quran to Muhammad.

tossups.p: In a famous hadith, a stranger in bright white clothes with jet-black hair sat knee to knee with Muhammad and asked him about Islam, faith, and the Last Hour. After the stranger left, Muhammad told Umar that this figure had come to teach them their religion.
tossups.r: Muslims believe this angel also brought the Quran to Muhammad. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: Muslim tradition says this figure went over the revelation with Muhammad every Ramadan, and twice in Muhammad’s final year. Muslims also identify this figure with the “Trustworthy Spirit” mentioned in the Quran, and the surah “The Cow” lists him beside Michael.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this archangel who, Muslims believe, brought the Quran down to Muhammad’s heart.

tossups.p: In John Milton’s _Paradise Lost_, this angel commands the guards at the eastern gate of Eden and sends Ithuriel [“ih-THOOR-ee-el”] and Zephon to search the garden for an intruder. When they bring Satan back to him, this angel confronts Satan, who finally flees.
tossups.r: In the Bible, this angel tells Mary that she will give birth to Jesus. For 10 points, name this archangel.

tossups.p: In Joseph Haydn’s oratorio _The Creation_, a soprano sings the part of this angel, who joins the angels Uriel and Raphael in describing the days of creation. A Jewish bedtime blessing asks for Michael to stand at the right side and this angel at the left.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this archangel who, in the Gospel of Luke, visits Mary in Nazareth.

tossups.p: Cole Porter’s musical _Anything Goes_ includes a song urging this angel to “blow.” A mathematical shape with a finite volume but an infinite surface area is named for this angel’s horn, from a Christian folk tradition that he will sound a trumpet on Judgment Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this archangel, who in the Gospel of Luke tells Mary she will give birth to Jesus.

tossups.p: This figure’s Hebrew name is often translated “God is my strength,” and Catholics honor him as a patron saint of messengers and communications workers. In the Gospel of Luke, this figure tells a doubting priest, “I stand in the presence of God.”
tossups.r: That priest’s son became John the Baptist. For 10 points, name this archangel who announced the birth of Jesus to Mary.

A shape with finite volume but infinite surface area is named for his horn; Cole Porter’s _Anything Goes_ has a song urging him to “blow”
His Hebrew name is often translated “God is my strength”; Catholics honor him as a patron saint of messengers and communications workers

trap.title: Which archangel?
trap.body: Gabriel shares the stage with other named angels. Michael is the warrior who battles the dragon in the Book of Revelation and protects Israel in the Book of Daniel; Raphael guides young Tobias in the Book of Tobit (and Raphael the Renaissance painter is a separate answer line); and in Islamic tradition, Israfil, not Gabriel, blows the trumpet on Judgment Day. The angels who speak to Joseph in his dreams and to the shepherds at Jesus’s birth are never named in the Gospels.
trap.fix: Messages and announcements (Daniel’s visions, Zechariah, Mary, and the revelation of the Quran) point to Gabriel, whom Muslims call Jibril; both names are accepted. Battles with the dragon in Revelation point to Michael, and healing or the Book of Tobit points to Raphael.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gabriel (or Jibril or Jibreel; accept Gavriel; do not accept “Michael” or “Raphael”)

topics.name: Gautama Buddha
topics.kicker: Founder of Buddhism · The prince who became the “Awakened One”
topics.briefing: Buddhist tradition says that Siddhartha Gautama was born a prince in Lumbini, in southern Nepal, and grew up surrounded by luxury until four sights (an old man, a sick man, a dead body, and a wandering holy man) sent him searching for the cause of suffering. After six years of hardship, he sat beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya and, Buddhists believe, reached enlightenment, becoming the Buddha, or “Awakened One.” He spent the next 45 years teaching across northern India.
topics.answerHtml: the Buddha (or Siddhartha Gautama, accepting either name; or Gautama Buddha; accept Shakyamuni; do not accept “Buddhism”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Before this man’s birth, his mother is said to have dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks entered her side. Because that mother, Queen Maya, died a week after his birth, he was raised by her sister Mahaprajapati [“muh-HAH-pruh-JAH-puh-tee”], who later became the first nun of his religion.
tossups.r: He was born in the grove of Lumbini. For 10 points, name this prince of the Shakya clan who founded Buddhism.

tossups.p: Soon after this man’s birth, the sage Asita [“uh-SEE-tuh”] wept because he knew he would not live to hear the child’s future teachings. Other wise men told this man’s father that his son would become either a great king or a great holy man.
tossups.r: He later left his palace to become a wandering holy man. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: This man’s father, Suddhodana [“sood-DOH-duh-nuh”], surrounded him with luxury so that he would never see suffering. On trips outside the palace, this man’s charioteer, Channa [“CHUN-nuh”], explained that every person grows old, falls sick, and dies.
tossups.r: Those Four Sights, which ended with a wandering holy man, led him to leave home. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: This man’s newborn son was named Rahula [“RAH-hoo-luh”], a name often explained as meaning “fetter,” because the prince felt the baby would tie him to the world. Soon afterward, this man slipped away at night on his horse, Kanthaka [“KUN-tuh-kuh”], leaving behind his wife, Yasodhara [“yah-SHOH-duh-ruh”].
tossups.r: He later reached enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: This man’s five fellow ascetics [“uh-SET-iks”] abandoned him in disgust when he gave up years of harsh fasting, during which he had become little more than skin and bones. On the day of his enlightenment, a young woman named Sujata [“soo-JAH-tuh”] gave him a bowl of rice cooked in milk.
tossups.r: He then taught a Middle Way between luxury and harsh self-denial. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: In Buddhist tradition, while this man sat in deep concentration through the night, the demon Mara [“MAH-ruh”] attacked him with armies and sent his daughters to tempt him. When Mara demanded proof of this man’s right to sit there, this man touched the ground and called on the earth as his witness.
tossups.r: He then reached enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: A sacred fig in Anuradhapura [“uh-NOO-ruh-DAH-puh-ruh”], Sri Lanka, is said to have grown from a branch of the tree this man sat beneath, carried there by Emperor Ashoka’s daughter Sanghamitta [“sung-guh-MIT-tuh”]. The Mahabodhi [“muh-hah-BOH-dee”] Temple marks the place where this man sat under the original tree.
tossups.r: There, at Bodh Gaya, he reached enlightenment. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: In a deer park near Varanasi [“vuh-RAH-nuh-see”], this man gave a sermon called “Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Dharma” to five former companions. One of those listeners, Kondanna [“KOHN-dun-nuh”], was the first to understand it.
tossups.r: That sermon at Sarnath first laid out the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: This teacher’s cousin and attendant, Ananda [“AH-nun-duh”], was famed for remembering every sermon, and recited them at a great council after this teacher’s death. At Ananda’s urging, this teacher allowed women to become nuns, starting with the aunt who raised him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this teacher who reached enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and founded Buddhism.

tossups.p: This teacher’s jealous cousin Devadatta [“DAY-vuh-DUT-tuh”] is said to have tried to kill him by rolling a boulder down a hill and by sending a maddened elephant named Nalagiri [“NAH-luh-GEE-ree”] charging toward him. According to tradition, this teacher calmed the elephant with loving-kindness.
tossups.r: This teacher had given his first sermon at Sarnath. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: The merchant Anathapindika [“uh-NAH-tuh-PIN-dih-kuh”] is said to have covered the ground of Prince Jeta’s grove with gold coins to buy it as a retreat for this teacher and his monks. This teacher spent many rainy seasons at that grove near the city of Shravasti [“shruh-VAHS-tee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this teacher whose title means “Awakened One,” the founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: Hundreds of Jataka [“JAH-tuh-kuh”] tales describe this man’s past lives as animals and people, including one as the generous Prince Vessantara [“vay-SAHN-tuh-ruh”], who gave away everything he owned. Some Hindu traditions count this man as an avatar of the god Vishnu.
tossups.r: Buddhists say that in his final life he was born a prince in Lumbini. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: This teacher’s last words urged his followers to strive on with diligence, because all things that come into being must pass away. He had fallen ill after eating a meal offered by Cunda [“CHOON-dah”] the smith, and he died at about age 80 at Kushinagar [“koo-shee-NAH-gar”], lying between two sal trees.
tossups.r: Reclining statues show him at that moment of final nirvana. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: In Japan, people celebrate this man’s birthday on April 8 by pouring sweet tea over small statues of him as a baby, pointing one hand up and the other down. An inscription on a pillar set up by Emperor Ashoka marks the grove of Lumbini, in southern Nepal, as his birthplace.
tossups.r: Many Buddhists also celebrate his birth on the full-moon festival of Vesak. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

tossups.p: Edwin Arnold’s long 1879 poem _The Light of Asia_ retells this man’s life. Statues of this man often show a rounded bump on top of his head, called an ushnisha [“oosh-NEE-shuh”], and long earlobes, said to have been stretched by the heavy earrings he wore as a prince.
tossups.r: Many statues show him seated cross-legged with his hands in his lap. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

trap.title: The man, not the religion
trap.body: Tossups about this man are full of clues about Buddhism itself, so it is easy to blurt “Buddhism” when the question asks for “this man” or “this teacher,” and that answer is wrong. Mahavira, Jainism’s 24th Tirthankara, is another trap: he was also a prince who gave up palace life in the same region at about the same time. Other buddhas, like Amitabha of the Pure Land or Maitreya, the buddha of the future, are different answers, and so is Bodhidharma, who is said to have brought Zen to China.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man,” “this prince,” or “this teacher” wants the Buddha; “this religion” wants Buddhism. The Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, Gautama Buddha, and Shakyamuni are all accepted. Clues about Vardhamana, the Tirthankaras, or the Digambara and Svetambara sects point to Mahavira instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: the Buddha (or Siddhartha Gautama, accepting either name; or Gautama Buddha; accept Shakyamuni; do not accept “Buddhism”)

topics.name: Joseph (son of Jacob)
topics.kicker: Dreamer sold into slavery by his brothers · Rose to power in Egypt
topics.briefing: In the Book of Genesis, Joseph was his father Jacob’s favorite son, and his jealous older brothers hated him for it, especially after Jacob gave him a special coat and Joseph dreamed that they would all bow down to him. The brothers sold him to traders headed for Egypt, where he rose from slave and prisoner to Pharaoh’s top official by explaining dreams. In the Quran, his story fills the twelfth surah, named Yusuf.
topics.answerHtml: Joseph (accept Yosef or Yusuf; do not accept “Jacob” or Joseph the husband of Mary)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Pharaoh gave this man the Egyptian name Zaphenath-paneah [“ZAF-uh-nath puh-NEE-uh”] and arranged his marriage to Asenath [“AS-uh-nath”], the daughter of a priest of On. This man named his firstborn son Manasseh [“muh-NASS-uh”], saying that God had made him forget all his hardship.
tossups.r: His father, Jacob, had once given him a coat of many colors. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who rose to power in Egypt.

tossups.p: This young man was sent to check on his brothers near Shechem [“SHEK-um”] but found them at Dothan [“DOH-thun”], where they plotted to kill him. They mocked him as “this dreamer” because he had dreamed that their sheaves of grain bowed down to his sheaf.
tossups.r: Instead, they sold him to traders bound for Egypt. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who wore a coat of many colors.

tossups.p: This man’s oldest brother, Reuben, talked the others out of killing him and secretly planned to rescue him from the dry pit they threw him into. Another brother, Judah, then suggested a way to profit from him instead.
tossups.r: The brothers sold him for twenty pieces of silver to traders headed for Egypt. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob and Rachel.

tossups.p: In the Quran’s telling, this man’s brothers claimed that a wolf ate him while they were off racing one another. In the Bible, they dipped his robe in a goat’s blood so that their father would believe a wild animal had killed him.
tossups.r: That robe was a coat of many colors. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob whose brothers sold him into slavery.

tossups.p: After buying this man as a slave, an Egyptian officer named Potiphar [“POT-ih-fur”] put him in charge of his entire household. When Potiphar’s wife falsely accused him, this man was thrown into prison, where the jailer soon put him in charge of the other prisoners.
tossups.r: In prison, he explained the dreams of two of Pharaoh’s servants. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who later explained Pharaoh’s dreams.

tossups.p: Two years after this man correctly predicted that a royal cupbearer would be freed, that cupbearer finally remembered him and told Pharaoh about him. In prison, this man had also said that a baker’s dream of three baskets of bread meant the baker would be put to death.
tossups.r: Pharaoh then sent for him to explain Pharaoh’s own dreams. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who rose to power in Egypt.

tossups.p: During a long famine, this man bought up nearly all the land of Egypt for its ruler, except the land of the priests. Earlier, he had advised that ruler to store one-fifth of every harvest in the good years before the famine.
tossups.r: He had predicted that famine by explaining Pharaoh’s dream of seven fat cows and seven thin cows. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob.

tossups.p: After naming this man his second-in-command, Pharaoh put his own signet ring on this man’s hand, dressed him in fine linen with a gold chain, and had him ride in a chariot while people cried, “Bow the knee!” This man was thirty years old at the time.
tossups.r: He had won that post by explaining Pharaoh’s dreams. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob.

tossups.p: This man accused his visiting brothers of being spies and kept Simeon as a hostage until they returned with their youngest brother. He also secretly had their silver put back into their sacks of grain before sending them home.
tossups.r: His brothers had come to Egypt to buy food during a famine, not knowing who he was. For 10 points, name this governor of Egypt, a son of Jacob.

tossups.p: This man had his silver cup hidden in his youngest brother’s sack of grain, then sent his steward to accuse the brothers of theft. When Judah offered to stay behind as a slave in that brother’s place, this man wept and revealed who he was.
tossups.r: That youngest brother was Benjamin. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob and Rachel who forgave the brothers who had sold him.

tossups.p: After their father died, this man’s brothers feared his revenge, but he told them, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” Earlier, he had settled his father’s whole family in the land of Goshen [“GOH-shen”].
tossups.r: Those brothers had once sold him into slavery. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who became a ruler in Egypt.

tossups.p: When this man brought his two sons to their dying grandfather, the old man crossed his arms to place his right hand on the head of the younger boy, Ephraim [“EE-free-um”]. Those two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each became the ancestor of a tribe of Israel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who was sold into Egypt by his jealous brothers.

tossups.p: Before he died at age 110, this man made the Israelites promise to carry his bones out of Egypt, and Moses took those bones with him during the Exodus. Jewish tradition calls this man “the Righteous,” or HaTzaddik [“hah-tsah-DEEK”].
tossups.r: His brothers had once sold him into slavery. For 10 points, name this son of Jacob who wore a coat of many colors.

tossups.p: One chapter of the Quran tells this prophet’s story from beginning to end and calls it “the most beautiful of stories.” In that version, his grieving father loses his sight from weeping and regains it when this man’s shirt is laid across his face.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this son of Jacob, the subject of the Quran’s twelfth surah.

tossups.p: The Persian poet Jami [“JAH-mee”] wrote a famous poem about this man and Zulaikha [“zoo-LY-khuh”], the name Islamic tradition gives to his master’s wife. Thomas Mann retold this man’s life in a series of four novels published between 1933 and 1943.
tossups.r: Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice’s musical about him features the song “Any Dream Will Do.” For 10 points, name this biblical dreamer with an “Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.”

clues.t: His father gave him a “coat of many colors” (in some translations, a long robe with sleeves)
His jealous brothers sold him into slavery, and traders carried him off to Egypt
Explained Pharaoh’s dreams of seven fat and seven thin cows: seven years of plenty, then seven years of famine
The favorite son of Jacob and the first son of Rachel; Benjamin was his only full brother
Hero of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice’s musical about his “Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat”
Dreamed that his brothers’ sheaves of grain bowed down to his sheaf, and later that the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him
Reuben saved his life, so the brothers threw him into a dry pit; at Judah’s suggestion, they sold him for 20 pieces of silver
The brothers dipped his robe in goat’s blood so their father would think a wild animal had killed him
Sold to Potiphar, an Egyptian officer; jailed after Potiphar’s wife falsely accused him
In prison, explained the dreams of Pharaoh’s cupbearer (freed in three days) and baker (put to death)
Became Pharaoh’s second-in-command at age 30 and stored grain to prepare Egypt for the famine
Hid his silver cup in Benjamin’s sack to test his brothers; Judah offered to become a slave in Benjamin’s place
His sons Ephraim and Manasseh each became the ancestor of a tribe of Israel; their grandfather blessed the younger, Ephraim, with his right hand
Surah 12 of the Quran, named for him, tells his whole story and calls it “the most beautiful” (or “the best”) of stories
Brought his father’s whole family to settle in the land of Goshen in Egypt
Pharaoh named him Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, daughter of a priest of On, as his wife
His brothers mocked him as “this dreamer” and plotted against him at Dothan, near Shechem
The freed cupbearer forgot about him for two years before telling Pharaoh about him
Pharaoh gave him a signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain, and a chariot; people cried “Bow the knee!”

Accused his brothers of being spies, kept Simeon as a hostage, and secretly put their silver back in their sacks
Forgave his brothers: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good”
Died at age 110; Moses carried his bones out of Egypt during the Exodus
Jewish tradition calls him “the Righteous” (HaTzaddik)
In the Quran, the brothers blame a wolf, and his father’s lost sight returns when his shirt is laid on his face
The Persian poet Jami wrote a famous poem about him and Zulaikha, his master’s wife in Islamic tradition
Thomas Mann retold his story in a series of four novels published from 1933 to 1943
Songs in the Lloyd Webber–Rice musical include “Any Dream Will Do” and “Close Every Door”

trap.title: Which Joseph? Which dreamer?
trap.body: Two Bible figures named Joseph both receive messages in dreams and both end up in Egypt. Joseph the son of Jacob wears the coat of many colors and explains Pharaoh’s dreams in the Book of Genesis; Joseph the husband of Mary is warned by an angel in dreams in the Gospel of Matthew and flees to Egypt with Mary and the baby Jesus. Jacob, his father, and Daniel, who explains King Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams in Babylon, are wrong answers too.
trap.fix: Genesis clues (Jacob, the brothers, the coat, Potiphar, Pharaoh, the famine, Benjamin) mean Joseph son of Jacob, called Yusuf in the Quran. Clues about Mary, Bethlehem, King Herod, or a carpenter mean the other Joseph, and a Babylonian king’s dream of a giant statue means Daniel.
trap.line: Real answer line: Joseph (accept Yosef or Yusuf; do not accept “Jacob” or Joseph the husband of Mary)

topics.name: Karma
topics.kicker: Idea that actions bring results · Shared by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs
topics.dates: Taught in India for more than 2,500 years
topics.briefing: Karma is a Sanskrit word meaning “action,” and it names the idea that every deed, good or bad, brings results for the person who does it, in this life or a future one. Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs all teach it, though in different ways: Jains picture it as sticky particles clinging to the soul, while Buddhists say what counts most is a person’s intention.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the _Brihadaranyaka Upanishad_ [“brih-hud-AR-un-yuh-kuh oo-PAN-ih-shud”], the sage Yajnavalkya [“yahj-nyah-VAHL-kyah”] teaches that a person becomes good through good deeds and bad through bad deeds. He adds that desire shapes a person’s will, will shapes deeds, and deeds shape what that person becomes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of cause and effect, from a Sanskrit word meaning “action.”

tossups.p: In the _Bhagavad Gita_, Krishna tells Arjuna he has a right to his actions but never to their fruits, and teaches a path of selfless action named for this concept. Krishna presents that path alongside the paths of devotion, or bhakti, and of knowledge, or jnana [“GYAH-nuh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this idea, found in Hinduism and Buddhism, that every deed brings consequences.

tossups.p: Some Hindu teachers divide this concept into three kinds: sanchita [“SUN-chih-tuh”], the store built up over past lives; prarabdha [“pruh-RAHB-duh”], the portion that bears fruit in this life; and agami [“AH-gah-mee”], the portion being created by present actions.
tossups.r: Hindus believe it binds the soul to the cycle of rebirth until it reaches moksha. For 10 points, name this law of moral cause and effect.

tossups.p: The Buddha declared that this concept is really intention, or cetana [“CHAY-tuh-nuh”], so only deliberate acts of body, speech, and mind produce it. Buddhists call its results vipaka [“vih-PAH-kuh”], meaning “ripening,” and compare them to fruit that grows from a planted seed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that good and bad actions bring good and bad results.

tossups.p: During the second watch of the night of his enlightenment, the Buddha is said to have seen countless beings dying and being born again in better or worse states according to this principle. In the first watch of that night, he is said to have remembered his own past lives.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of cause and effect, a Sanskrit word for “action” or “deed.”

tossups.p: One religion sorts this force into eight main types and calls its inflow into the soul asrava [“AHS-ruh-vuh”] and its shedding nirjara [“nir-JAH-ruh”]. That religion teaches that this force is made of tiny particles of matter that cling to the soul, or jiva [“JEE-vuh”], the way dust clings to a body smeared with oil.
tossups.r: Jains try to shed all of it to free the soul. For 10 points, name this concept, from a Sanskrit word meaning “action.”

tossups.p: Guru Nanak’s Japji [“JUP-jee”] describes this force by teaching that people reap what they themselves have sown. Sikhs believe that it shapes a person’s rebirth, but that liberation comes only through God’s grace, called nadar [“NUH-dur”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of cause and effect that Sikhs share with Hindus, Buddhists, and Jains.

tossups.p: Hindus and Jains often speak of two kinds of this force: punya [“POON-yuh”], or merit, and papa [“PAH-puh”], or demerit. Buddhists in Thailand and Laos make merit by placing food in the bowls of monks on their morning alms rounds, hoping to improve this force.
tossups.r: Good and bad deeds are thought to shape a person’s next life. For 10 points, name this principle that deeds bring matching results.

tossups.p: In the earliest Vedas, this word mostly meant the correct performance of sacrifices and other rituals, a meaning stressed by the Mimamsa [“mee-MAHM-suh”] school of Hindu philosophy. Later texts turned it into a moral law that helps explain samsara [“sum-SAH-ruh”], the cycle of rebirth.
tossups.r: Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs all teach versions of it. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit word meaning “action” or “deed.”

tossups.p: In the Tibetan Wheel of Life, a ring around the center shows people rising on a white half and falling on a black half, to stand for good and bad forms of this force. The whole wheel is gripped by Yama [“YAH-muh”], the lord of death.
tossups.r: Buddhists believe this force helps decide where beings are reborn. For 10 points, name this principle of cause and effect.

tossups.p: The opening verse of the _Dhammapada_ [“DAH-muh-PAH-duh”] says that suffering follows a person who speaks or acts with an impure mind, just as a cart’s wheel follows the foot of the ox that pulls it. Buddhists see that verse as a lesson about this force.
tossups.r: Its name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning “action.” For 10 points, name this law that good and bad deeds bring matching results.

tossups.p: In Hindu tradition, the scribe Chitragupta [“chit-ruh-GOOP-tuh”] records the good and bad deeds that make up each person’s store of this force, so that Yama, the god of death, can judge each soul. Many Hindus believe this force decides what kind of life a soul enters next.
tossups.r: Its name means “action” in Sanskrit. For 10 points, name this law of moral cause and effect.

tossups.p: Swami Vivekananda [“vih-VAY-kah-NUN-duh”] turned lectures he had given in New York into a book about a yoga named for this concept, teaching that work done without selfish motives frees the soul. He drew that teaching from the _Bhagavad Gita_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this concept, which teaches that every action has consequences in this life and the next.

tossups.p: Jains teach that the Tirthankaras [“teer-TUN-kuh-ruz”] reached perfect knowledge only after destroying the four most harmful types of this, which cloud the soul’s knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. Jain monks keep strict vows to stop new amounts of it from flowing in, and they fast to burn away what has already built up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that Jains picture as a sticky substance clinging to the soul.

tossups.p: John Lennon’s 1970 hit single put the word “Instant” in front of this concept, and Culture Club’s 1983 number-one song paired it with a color-changing lizard. In the late 1800s, the Theosophical Society helped spread this idea, along with belief in past lives, to Europeans and Americans.
tossups.r: Its name is a Sanskrit word for “action.” For 10 points, name this concept, often summed up as “what goes around comes around.”

clues.t: From a Sanskrit word meaning “action” or “deed”: the law that every action brings a result
Taught in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism
Believers hold that good and bad deeds shape a person’s future, including the next life in the cycle of rebirth (samsara)
In everyday English, it means “what goes around comes around”
In the _Bhagavad Gita_, Krishna teaches the yoga of selfless action: do your duty without attachment to its fruits
The _Gita_’s three paths: selfless action, jnana (knowledge), and bhakti (devotion)
Jains see it as sticky, invisible particles of matter that cling to the soul (jiva); shedding them all frees the soul
Escaping its hold brings moksha (in Hinduism and Jainism) or nirvana (in Buddhism)
In Buddhism, the Buddha said it is really intention (cetana), so only deliberate acts count
Good deeds are said to bring merit (punya) and bad deeds demerit (papa); Buddhists make merit by giving food to monks
In Sikhism, it shapes a soul’s rebirth, but liberation comes only through God’s grace (nadar)
In the _Brihadaranyaka Upanishad_, the sage Yajnavalkya says one becomes good by good deeds and bad by bad deeds
Three kinds in Hindu teaching: sanchita (stored up), prarabdha (ripening now), and agami (being made now)
Buddhists call its results vipaka (“ripening”), like fruit growing from a seed
In the second watch of his enlightenment night, the Buddha is said to have seen beings reborn according to their deeds
Jain terms: asrava (inflow), bandha (bondage), samvara (stopping), and nirjara (shedding)
Jains name eight main types; the Tirthankaras destroyed the four most harmful ones before reaching perfect knowledge
Guru Nanak’s Japji says people reap what they themselves have sown
In the earliest Vedas it mostly meant correct ritual action; the Mimamsa school stressed that meaning
Tibetan Wheel of Life: a ring shows beings rising on a white half and falling on a black half; Yama grips the wheel
The _Dhammapada_’s first verse: suffering follows an impure mind as a cart’s wheel follows the ox
In Hindu tradition, the scribe Chitragupta records each person’s deeds for Yama, the god of death
Swami Vivekananda’s book of New York lectures explained the yoga of selfless work
The Theosophical Society spread it in the West in the late 1800s; songs by John Lennon (1970) and Culture Club (1983) used the word

trap.title: Action, not the cycle
trap.body: Karma, dharma, samsara, and moksha all turn up in the same Hindu and Buddhist tossups, and they sound alike. Karma is the force of a person’s actions; samsara is the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth that karma keeps turning; dharma is duty or the Buddha’s teaching; and moksha or nirvana is the escape. Reincarnation is the rebirth itself, not the law that shapes it, so “reincarnation” is wrong here.
trap.fix: Listen for deeds, fruits, merit, or cause and effect: that is karma. “This cycle” or “this wheel” means samsara, “this duty” means dharma, and “this liberation” means moksha or nirvana. The Pali form, kamma, is accepted.
trap.line: Real answer line: karma (or kamma; do not accept “dharma,” “samsara,” or “reincarnation”)

topics.name: King David
topics.kicker: Shepherd boy who defeated Goliath · Second king of Israel, father of Solomon
topics.briefing: In the Bible’s story, a shepherd boy named David steps forward when no soldier dares to fight the Philistine giant Goliath, and he brings the giant down with a single stone from his sling. David goes on to become the second king of Israel, makes Jerusalem his capital, and is traditionally credited with writing many of the Psalms. Muslims honor him as the prophet Dawud.
topics.answerHtml: David (accept King David or Dawud; do not accept “Goliath,” “Saul,” or “Solomon”; do not accept Michelangelo’s statue)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When the prophet Samuel thought that the tall Eliab [“ee-LY-ab”] must be God’s chosen king, God told him that people look at outward appearance, but God looks at the heart. Samuel passed over seven brothers before calling in this man, the youngest, who was out tending sheep.
tossups.r: Samuel then anointed this son of Jesse with oil. For 10 points, name this shepherd who became king of Israel.

tossups.p: Saul’s servant described this young man as skillful in playing, brave in battle, and wise in speech. Whenever a harmful spirit troubled Saul, this man played the lyre for him, and the spirit would leave.
tossups.r: Later, the jealous Saul hurled a spear at him while he played. For 10 points, name this harp-playing shepherd who defeated Goliath.

tossups.p: In the Valley of Elah [“EE-luh”], this young man refused to wear King Saul’s armor and helmet, saying he was not used to them, and instead chose five smooth stones from a brook. He told his opponent that he came in the name of the Lord, not with sword and spear.
tossups.r: With one stone from his sling, he defeated the giant Goliath. For 10 points, name this shepherd who became king of Israel.

tossups.p: This man’s wife Michal [“mee-KHAHL”], a king’s daughter, helped him escape through a window and put a household idol in his bed to fool her father’s messengers. Her father had turned against this man after women sang that he had slain ten thousands to the king’s thousands.
tossups.r: That king was Saul. For 10 points, name this man who succeeded Saul as king of Israel.

tossups.p: This man’s closest friend gave him his own robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt, and later warned him of danger by shooting arrows in a field. When that friend died in battle on Mount Gilboa [“gil-BOH-uh”], this man mourned with a lament whose refrain is “How the mighty have fallen!”
tossups.r: That friend was Jonathan, the son of King Saul. For 10 points, name this king of Israel.

tossups.p: While hiding in a cave at En Gedi [“en GED-ee”], this man secretly cut off a corner of King Saul’s robe but refused to harm “the Lord’s anointed.” Another night, he crept into Saul’s camp and took the sleeping king’s spear and water jug instead of killing him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who became king of Israel after Saul and made Jerusalem his capital.

tossups.p: This king captured the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites [“JEB-yoo-sites”], and the fortress was renamed in his honor. He later danced with all his might as the Ark of the Covenant was carried into his new capital, while his wife Michal watched and scorned him.
tossups.r: That capital was Jerusalem, where his son Solomon later built the Temple. For 10 points, name this king of Israel.

tossups.p: The prophet Nathan told this king about a rich man who took a poor man’s only lamb, then declared, “You are the man!” Nathan was rebuking this king for taking Bathsheba as his wife after arranging the death of her husband, Uriah [“yoo-RY-uh”].
tossups.r: Their son Solomon became the next king. For 10 points, name this king of Israel.

tossups.p: William Faulkner’s novel _Absalom, Absalom!_ echoes this king’s cry of grief for a rebellious son, who was killed by the general Joab after his head caught in the branches of an oak tree. That son had driven this king out of Jerusalem in a revolt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this king of Israel, traditionally credited with writing many of the Psalms.

tossups.p: Tradition holds that this king wrote the fifty-first poem in one biblical book as a plea for mercy after the prophet Nathan rebuked him. Seventy-three poems in that book carry headings linking them to this king, including one that begins, “The Lord is my shepherd.”
tossups.r: That book is the Psalms. For 10 points, name this shepherd-king of Israel who defeated Goliath.

tossups.p: The Quran says that God made the mountains and the birds join this prophet in praising God, and softened iron for him so that he could make coats of armor. Muslims believe God gave this prophet the Zabur [“zah-BOOR”], a holy book identified with the Psalms.
tossups.r: In the Bible, he kills the giant Goliath. For 10 points, name this king of Israel.

tossups.p: The Book of Ruth ends with a family tree showing that Ruth and Boaz were this man’s great-grandparents. The Gospel of Luke says that Joseph traveled to Bethlehem, called this man’s city, because Joseph was descended from this man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this king of Israel whom the Gospels name as an ancestor of Jesus.

tossups.p: When three of his mighty warriors broke through Philistine lines to bring him water from the well at Bethlehem, this leader refused to drink it and poured it out as an offering to God. He also let his late friend Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth [“meh-FIB-oh-sheth”] eat at the royal table.
tossups.r: As a young shepherd, he had defeated Goliath. For 10 points, name this king of Israel, the father of Solomon.

tossups.p: An Aramaic inscription found at Tel Dan in northern Israel in 1993 mentions the “House of” this king, one of the oldest known references to him outside the Bible. Jewish tradition holds that the Messiah will be one of this king’s descendants.
tossups.r: A six-pointed star on Israel’s flag is named for him. For 10 points, name this king of Israel.

tossups.p: Gian Lorenzo Bernini [“bair-NEE-nee”] sculpted this figure twisting his body and biting his lip as he prepares to hurl a stone. Leonard Cohen’s song “Hallelujah” begins by describing a “secret chord” that this man played to please the Lord.
tossups.r: Michelangelo’s giant marble statue of him stands in Florence. For 10 points, name this biblical king.

clues.t: As a young shepherd, defeated the Philistine giant Goliath with a sling and a stone
Second king of Israel, after Saul, and the father of Solomon
Traditionally credited with writing many of the Psalms, including Psalm 23 (“The Lord is my shepherd”)
Made Jerusalem his capital and brought the Ark of the Covenant there
The six-pointed star on Israel’s flag is named for him
The prophet Samuel anointed him, the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, after passing over his older brothers
Played the lyre (harp) to soothe King Saul; the jealous Saul hurled a spear at him
Best friend of Saul’s son Jonathan; when Saul and Jonathan died on Mount Gilboa, he lamented, “How the mighty have fallen!”
Women sang that Saul had slain his thousands, but he had slain his ten thousands, which made Saul jealous
Took Bathsheba as his wife after arranging the death of her husband, Uriah; the prophet Nathan rebuked him: “You are the man!”
His son Absalom led a revolt; he mourned, “O my son Absalom, my son, my son!”
Muslims honor him as a prophet who received the Zabur (identified with the Psalms) and killed Goliath (Jalut)
The Gospels trace Jesus’s family line back to him; Bethlehem is called his city
Captured the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites and danced before the Ark as it entered Jerusalem
God told Samuel, who thought Eliab was the chosen one, that people look at appearance but God looks at the heart
Fought in the Valley of Elah; refused Saul’s armor and chose five smooth stones from a brook; Goliath came from Gath
His wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, helped him escape through a window and put an idol in his bed; she later scorned his dancing
Spared Saul in a cave at En Gedi, cutting off a corner of his robe; later took the sleeping Saul’s spear and water jug
Ruled Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years before ruling all Israel; reigned 40 years in all
Psalm 51 is traditionally his plea for mercy after Nathan’s rebuke; 73 psalms carry his name in their headings
William Faulkner’s novel _Absalom, Absalom!_ echoes his cry of grief; Joab killed Absalom after his head caught in an oak
The Quran says God softened iron for him to make armor and had the mountains and birds praise God with him
In 2 Samuel, the prophet Nathan tells him that his son, not he, will build the Temple, and that God will make his royal line last forever
Great-grandson of Ruth and Boaz, according to the family tree that ends the Book of Ruth
Poured out the water three mighty warriors brought from Bethlehem’s well; welcomed Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth to his table
The Tel Dan inscription, found in 1993, refers to his royal house; Jewish tradition says the Messiah will descend from him
Sculpted by Michelangelo (a marble giant in Florence), Donatello (in bronze), and Bernini (biting his lip as he hurls a stone)
Leonard Cohen’s song “Hallelujah” describes the “secret chord” he played to please the Lord

trap.title: The king, not the giant
trap.body: David tossups are crowded with other people. Goliath is the giant he defeated; Saul is the first king, who hurled a spear at him; Jonathan is his best friend; Solomon is his son, who built the Temple; and Absalom is the son who rebelled. Michelangelo’s statue in Florence is its own Fine Arts answer line on this site, so a question that asks for “this sculpture” wants the statue, not the king.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man,” “this king,” or “this shepherd” plus the sling, the lyre, Jerusalem, Bathsheba, or the Psalms: that is David. In questions about Islam, his Arabic name, Dawud, is accepted. If the question says “this giant” or “this Philistine,” the answer is Goliath.
trap.line: Real answer line: David (accept King David or Dawud; do not accept “Goliath,” “Saul,” or “Solomon”; do not accept Michelangelo’s statue)

topics.name: Meditation
topics.kicker: Training the mind to be calm and focused · Practiced across many faiths
topics.briefing: Since ancient times, people of many faiths have sat in silence to calm and focus their minds. Buddhists believe the Buddha reached enlightenment while meditating under a fig tree, and Hindu, Jain, Sufi, and Sikh traditions all teach their own forms of meditation. In 1968 the Beatles traveled to India to learn it, and scientists have since studied whether it can ease stress.
topics.answerHtml: meditation (accept word forms like meditating; accept dhyana; prompt on yoga; do not accept “prayer”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In Patanjali’s [“puh-TUN-juh-lee’z”] _Yoga Sutras_, this practice is the seventh of eight limbs, coming after dharana [“DAR-uh-nuh”], or concentration, and before samadhi [“suh-MAH-dee”], or total absorption. Those sutras define yoga as the stilling of the movements of the mind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of calming and focusing the mind, often done sitting cross-legged in silence.

tossups.p: The school names Chan [“CHAHN”] in China and Zen in Japan both come from the Sanskrit word for this practice. Dogen [“DOH-gen”] taught a form of it called shikantaza [“shee-KAHN-tah-zah”], or “just sitting,” and Zen students also do it while walking, in a form called kinhin [“KIN-hin”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, Zen Buddhists practice zazen, a seated form of what mind-calming practice?

tossups.p: S. N. Goenka [“GOYN-kuh”], who learned from a teacher in Burma, led ten-day silent courses in vipassana [“vih-PAH-suh-nuh”], or “insight,” a form of this practice. Buddhists often pair vipassana with samatha [“SUH-muh-tuh”], or “calm,” which steadies the mind on a single object such as the breath.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice that the Buddha was doing beneath the Bodhi tree when he reached enlightenment.

tossups.p: The _Satipatthana Sutta_ [“suh-tee-PAHT-tah-nuh SOOT-tuh”] teaches four foundations for one form of this practice: the body, feelings, the mind, and mental objects. Buddhists also practice metta [“MET-tuh”], a form that wishes loving-kindness to all beings, and anapanasati [“AH-nah-pah-nuh-SUT-ee”], which follows the breath.
tossups.r: Those four foundations describe mindfulness. For 10 points, name this practice of focused attention, done in Zen as zazen.

tossups.p: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn founded a stress-reduction program at the University of Massachusetts Medical School that taught a nonreligious form of this practice. He described its key skill as paying attention, on purpose, to the present moment without judging it.
tossups.r: That skill is called mindfulness. For 10 points, name this practice of calming and focusing the mind.

tossups.p: John Lennon wrote “Dear Prudence” about Prudence Farrow, who did this practice so intensely that she would hardly leave her room. She and the Beatles had come to Rishikesh [“RISH-ih-kesh”], India, in 1968 to learn it from Maharishi Mahesh Yogi.
tossups.r: The Maharishi’s form of it is called Transcendental. For 10 points, name this mind-calming practice that often uses a repeated mantra.

tossups.p: Jains practice a 48-minute form of this activity called samayika [“SAH-mah-yee-kuh”], and a giant Jain statue of Bahubali [“BAH-hoo-bah-lee”] shows him doing it standing, so still that vines wrap around his legs. The Hindu god Shiva burned the love god Kama to ashes for disturbing his practice of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of stilling the mind, which the Buddha did beneath the Bodhi tree.

tossups.p: Sufis practice muraqaba [“moo-RAH-kuh-buh”], or “watchfulness,” a form of this activity, and they gather for dhikr [“ZIK-er”], the rhythmic repetition of God’s names. Members of the Mevlevi [“MEV-leh-vee”] order turn in a spinning ceremony that some describe as this practice in motion.
tossups.r: Those members are the “whirling dervishes.” For 10 points, name this practice of stilling and focusing the mind.

tossups.p: In the _Zhuangzi_ [“JWAHNG-dzuh”], Confucius’s student Yan Hui describes “sitting and forgetting,” in which he lets go of his body and his knowledge until he becomes one with the Way. That early Daoist form of this practice so impressed Confucius that he asked to become Yan Hui’s follower.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of quieting the mind, which Hindus, Buddhists, and Jains all teach.

tossups.p: Sikhs practice naam simran [“NAHM SIM-run”], a form of this activity in which they repeat the word Waheguru [“wah-hay-GOO-roo”] to keep God’s name in mind. Guru Nanak named remembering God’s name as one of a believer’s three main duties, along with honest work and sharing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of calming the mind, often done with a repeated word or sound called a mantra.

tossups.p: Paramahansa Yogananda [“puh-ruh-muh-HUN-suh YOH-guh-NUN-duh”] described a method of this practice called Kriya [“KREE-yuh”] Yoga in his 1946 book _Autobiography of a Yogi_. The sage Ramana Maharshi [“RAH-muh-nuh mah-HAR-shee”] taught a form of it built around a single question: “Who am I?”
tossups.r: Hindus often begin it by chanting Om. For 10 points, name this practice of stilling the mind, often done sitting in the lotus position.

tossups.p: Tibetan Buddhists may use a mandala, a circular design that often pictures a deity’s palace, as a focus for this practice. Many people do it in padmasana [“pud-MAH-suh-nuh”], a cross-legged pose with each foot resting on the opposite thigh.
tossups.r: That pose is called the lotus position. For 10 points, name this practice of calming the mind, in which a person may repeat a mantra.

tossups.p: In 1975, the Harvard doctor Herbert Benson published _The Relaxation Response_, a book that grew out of his studies of people who practiced a form of this activity. Since then, scientists have studied whether this practice affects stress, attention, and blood pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of calming and focusing the mind, often done while paying attention to the breath.

tossups.p: Legend says Bodhidharma [“BOH-dee-DAR-muh”] spent nine years doing this practice while facing a cave wall. Centuries later, the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh [“tick-nyaht-HAHN”] taught a slow walking form of it at Plum Village, the community he founded in France.
tossups.r: Both were teachers of Zen, whose name comes from a word for this practice. For 10 points, name this practice of calming the mind.

tossups.p: Statues of the Buddha often show his hands resting in his lap, one on top of the other with the thumbs touching, in a gesture named for this practice. Japanese Zen temples built dry rock gardens, like the one at Ryoan-ji [“ryoh-AHN-jee”], as aids to this practice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice of stilling and focusing the mind, often done in silence.

clues.t: A practice of calming and focusing the mind, often by sitting quietly and paying attention to the breath
Buddhists believe the Buddha reached enlightenment doing it under the Bodhi tree
Zen’s name comes from the Sanskrit word for it; zazen is its seated form in Zen Buddhism
Often done sitting cross-legged in the lotus position
Some forms repeat a sacred sound, word, or phrase called a mantra, such as Om
Buddhist forms include vipassana (“insight”) and samatha (“calm”)
Mindfulness: paying attention to the present moment, on purpose and without judging
Seventh of the eight limbs of yoga in Patanjali’s _Yoga Sutras_, between dharana (concentration) and samadhi (absorption)
Maharishi Mahesh Yogi taught a “Transcendental” form; the Beatles studied with him in Rishikesh, India, in 1968
Jon Kabat-Zinn founded a stress-reduction program at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in 1979
Metta: a Buddhist practice of loving-kindness that wishes happiness to all beings
Sufis practice muraqaba (“watchfulness”) and dhikr, the repetition of God’s names
Sikhs practice naam simran, repeating God’s name, Waheguru
It can also be done while walking, as in Zen kinhin or Thich Nhat Hanh’s walking practice
Dogen taught shikantaza (“just sitting”), a seated form with no object of focus
S. N. Goenka, who learned from a teacher in Burma, led ten-day silent vipassana courses
The _Satipatthana Sutta_ lists four foundations of mindfulness; anapanasati follows the breath
John Lennon’s “Dear Prudence” is about Prudence Farrow, who practiced so intensely she hardly left her room
Jains practice samayika, a 48-minute session; Bahubali’s statue shows him practicing standing, wrapped in vines
The Hindu god Shiva burned the love god Kama to ashes for disturbing his practice
The Mevlevi order’s “whirling dervishes” turn in a ceremony some describe as this practice in motion
Daoist “sitting and forgetting”: in the _Zhuangzi_, Yan Hui’s practice so impresses Confucius that he asks to follow him
Paramahansa Yogananda described Kriya Yoga in _Autobiography of a Yogi_ (1946)
Ramana Maharshi’s self-inquiry centers on one question: “Who am I?”
Tibetan Buddhists may focus on a mandala; padmasana is the lotus pose, with each foot on the opposite thigh
Herbert Benson’s _The Relaxation Response_ (1975); scientists have studied whether it affects stress
Legend says Bodhidharma did it while facing a cave wall for nine years
Buddha statues rest the hands in the lap, thumbs touching, in a mudra named for it; Ryoan-ji’s rock garden is an aid to it

trap.title: Not prayer, not yoga
trap.body: Meditation, prayer, and yoga often appear together, and quiz bowl answer lines keep them apart. Prayer means speaking to God or another divine being, often in words, while meditation trains calm and attention, often in silence or with a mantra. Yoga is a larger system in which meditation is only one of eight limbs, and Zen is a school of Buddhism, not the practice itself. Marcus Aurelius’s book _Meditations_ is a different answer line, too.
trap.fix: Listen for the breath, attention, a mantra, zazen, vipassana, or mindfulness: that is meditation. If the clues describe addressing God, such as salat or the Lord’s Prayer, say prayer. If you say “yoga,” expect a prompt for something more specific.
trap.line: Real answer line: meditation (accept word forms like meditating; accept dhyana; prompt on yoga; do not accept “prayer”)

topics.name: Prayer
topics.kicker: Speaking to God or the divine · Practiced in nearly every religion
topics.dates: Found in religions around the world
topics.briefing: Five times a day, Muslims face Mecca for salat; three times a day, many Jews recite the Amidah facing Jerusalem; and Christians around the world say the prayer Jesus taught, beginning “Our Father.” Prayer, the act of speaking to God or another divine power, takes many forms: Tibetan Buddhists spin prayer wheels, many Hindus chant mantras at dawn, and many Sikhs begin each morning with Guru Nanak’s Japji.
topics.answerHtml: prayer (accept word forms like praying; prompt on worship; do not accept “meditation” or a specific prayer such as the “Lord’s Prayer”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The most important example of this act in Jewish services is the Amidah [“ah-mee-DAH”], or “standing,” which worshippers recite three times a day while facing Jerusalem. The Amidah’s other name, Shemoneh Esrei [“sh’MOH-neh ESS-ray”], means “eighteen,” for the number of blessings it originally had.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God, which Muslims perform five times a day as salat.

tossups.p: Small leather boxes called tefillin [“t’FIL-in”], which many Jewish men wear on the arm and head during this act on weekday mornings, hold handwritten passages that include the Shema [“shuh-MAH”]. The Shema begins, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”
tossups.r: Public forms of this act in Judaism traditionally require a minyan [“MIN-yun”] of ten. For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God.

tossups.p: Before performing this act, Muslims wash their hands, face, arms, and feet in a ritual called wudu [“woo-DOO”]. Each performance is made up of units called rak’ahs [“RAK-ahz”], which include bowing and touching the forehead to the ground, and a muezzin [“moo-EZ-in”] calls believers to it from a minaret.
tossups.r: Muslims perform it five times a day, facing Mecca. For 10 points, name this act of worship, called salat in Arabic.

tossups.p: Muslim tradition says that during the Night Journey, God first required fifty of these acts each day, but Moses urged Muhammad to go back again and again to ask for fewer. Muslims also gather at mosques at midday on Fridays for a group form of this act called Jumu’ah [“JOO-moo-ah”].
tossups.r: The number finally fell to five a day. For 10 points, name this act, called salat in Arabic, that Muslims perform facing Mecca.

tossups.p: Protestant churches often end one famous example of this act with “For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever,” words missing from the oldest Gospel manuscripts. Jesus taught that example in the Sermon on the Mount, and it asks God to “give us this day our daily bread.”
tossups.r: It begins “Our Father, who art in heaven.” For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God.

tossups.p: Catholics count the steps of one devotion of this kind on a loop of beads divided into five groups of ten, called decades, while reflecting on the Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious, or Luminous Mysteries. Each bead in a decade stands for one Hail Mary.
tossups.r: That devotion is the rosary. For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God or to holy figures.

tossups.p: Tibetan Buddhists spin wheels named for this act, which are filled with scrolls printed with the mantra “Om mani padme hum” [“ohm MAH-nee PAHD-may HOOM”], believing each turn spreads the same blessing as reciting it. They also hang colorful flags named for this act so the wind can carry the blessings away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of addressing God or holy beings, which Muslims perform five times a day.

tossups.p: Hindus and Buddhists count repetitions of a mantra on a mala [“MAH-luh”] of 108 beads, and many Muslims use 33 or 99 beads to repeat praises of God. Eastern Orthodox Christians use a knotted rope during a form of this act that repeats “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.”
tossups.r: Strings of beads used this way are named for this act. For 10 points, name this act of addressing God.

tossups.p: Many Sikhs begin each morning by reciting Guru Nanak’s Japji Sahib [“JUP-jee SAH-hib”], the first composition in their holy book, and they end services with the Ardas [“ur-DAHS”], a form of this act said while standing with folded hands. Japji is the first of the daily recitations called Nitnem [“NIT-nem”], or “daily rule.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of addressing God, which Sikhs, Jews, Christians, and Muslims all practice.

tossups.p: Zoroastrians divide each day into five periods called gahs [“GAHZ”] for this act, and they untie and retie a sacred cord called the kusti [“KUSH-tee”] around the waist while doing it. They usually face a fire or another source of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of worship, which Muslims also perform five times a day.

tossups.p: At many Shinto shrines, worshippers ring a bell, bow twice, clap twice, and bow once more as they perform this act before the kami [“KAH-mee”]. Visitors may also write their wishes on small wooden plaques called ema [“EH-mah”] and hang them at the shrine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of addressing gods or spirits, also practiced in churches, mosques, and synagogues.

tossups.p: A 1508 ink drawing by Albrecht Dürer [“DYUR-er”] of a pair of folded hands became a famous symbol of this act. In the Gospels, Jesus does this in the Garden of Gethsemane [“geth-SEM-uh-nee”] on the night before his death, asking that “this cup” pass from him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God, often done with bowed head and folded hands.

tossups.p: Many Hindus recite the Gayatri [“GAH-yuh-tree”] Mantra, a verse from the Rig Veda addressed to the sun god Savitr [“SAH-vih-tur”], at dawn as an act of this kind. During aarti [“AR-tee”], worshippers wave small lamps before a sacred image while singing.
tossups.r: Hindus also offer flowers and food in worship called puja. For 10 points, name this act of addressing a god, which Muslims perform as salat.

tossups.p: The Liturgy of the Hours sets times for this act throughout the day, from Lauds at dawn to Vespers in the evening and Compline before sleep. Benedictine monks are known for a Latin motto that pairs this act with work.
tossups.r: That motto is “ora et labora.” For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God, a central part of Christian worship.

tossups.p: In the First Book of Samuel, a woman named Hannah moved her lips without making a sound while doing this at the shrine at Shiloh, and the priest Eli thought she was drunk. Visitors to Jerusalem’s Western Wall tuck written notes of this kind into its cracks.
tossups.r: Hannah later gave birth to the prophet Samuel. For 10 points, name this act of speaking to God.

clues.t: An act of speaking to God or another divine power, to praise, give thanks, or ask for help
Muslims perform salat five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca
Jesus taught the “Our Father,” which begins “Our Father, who art in heaven,” in the Sermon on the Mount
Many faiths count repetitions on strings of beads, such as the Catholic rosary and the Hindu and Buddhist mala
Believers may kneel, bow, stand, or fold their hands while doing it
Before salat, Muslims wash in a ritual called wudu; each salat is made of units called rak’ahs, with bowing and prostration
A muezzin calls believers from a minaret; Muslims gather at midday on Fridays for Jumu’ah
Judaism’s Amidah (“standing”) is recited three times a day, facing Jerusalem
The Shema: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one”
The rosary: five decades of Hail Marys while reflecting on the Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious, or Luminous Mysteries
Tibetan Buddhists spin wheels and hang flags carrying mantras such as “Om mani padme hum”
Many Sikhs recite Guru Nanak’s Japji Sahib each morning and say the Ardas, standing, at the end of services
Many Hindus recite the Gayatri Mantra at dawn; in aarti, they wave lamps before a sacred image
Public worship in Judaism traditionally requires a minyan, a group of ten
The Amidah’s other name, Shemoneh Esrei (“eighteen”), counts its original blessings
Tefillin, leather boxes worn on the arm and head on weekday mornings, hold passages that include the Shema
Muslim tradition: on the Night Journey, the daily number fell from fifty to five after Moses urged Muhammad to ask for fewer
The ending “For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory” is missing from the oldest Gospel manuscripts
Orthodox Christians use a knotted rope while repeating “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me”
Many Muslims use strings of 33 or 99 beads to repeat praises of God
Zoroastrians use five daily periods (gahs) and retie the sacred kusti cord, facing fire or light
At Shinto shrines: ring a bell, bow twice, clap twice, bow once; wishes go on wooden ema plaques
Albrecht Dürer’s 1508 ink drawing of folded hands became a famous symbol of it
In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asked that “this cup” pass from him
The Liturgy of the Hours runs from Lauds at dawn to Vespers and Compline; Benedictines pair it with work in “ora et labora”
In 1 Samuel, Hannah moved her lips silently at Shiloh, and the priest Eli thought she was drunk
Visitors tuck written notes into the cracks of Jerusalem’s Western Wall
The Gayatri Mantra, a verse of the Rig Veda, is addressed to the sun god Savitr

trap.title: Prayer or meditation?
trap.body: Prayer and meditation often show up in the same religion tossups. Prayer means addressing God or another divine power, often in words, as in salat, the Amidah, or the Lord’s Prayer; meditation trains calm and attention, often in silence. Specific prayers like the Lord’s Prayer, the Shema, or the Hail Mary, and objects like prayer beads or prayer wheels, are answers of their own, so they are wrong when the question wants the act itself.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this act” or “this practice” of speaking to God means prayer. “This prayer” means one particular text, so name it (the Lord’s Prayer, the Shema, the Amidah). Breathing, mantras for calm, and zazen point to meditation.
trap.line: Real answer line: prayer (accept word forms like praying; prompt on worship; do not accept “meditation” or a specific prayer such as the “Lord’s Prayer”)

topics.name: Reincarnation
topics.kicker: Belief in the soul’s return in a new body · From India to ancient Greece
topics.dates: Taught since ancient times in India and Greece
topics.briefing: Imagine being two years old and hearing that you are a great teacher who has returned in a new body. In 1937, Tibetan Buddhists believed exactly that about a little boy whom they recognized as the fourteenth Dalai Lama. Reincarnation, the belief that after death a soul is born again in a new body, is central to Hinduism, and Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs, the Druze, and Greek thinkers like Pythagoras and Plato have taught versions of it.
topics.answerHtml: reincarnation (accept rebirth, transmigration of souls, or metempsychosis; do not accept “samsara,” “karma,” “resurrection,” or “nirvana”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the _Bhagavad Gita_, Krishna tells Arjuna that death is certain for those who are born, and birth is certain for those who die. He compares this process to a person throwing away worn-out clothes and putting on new ones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that the soul is born again into a new body after death.

tossups.p: The _Brihadaranyaka Upanishad_ [“brih-hud-AR-un-yuh-kuh oo-PAN-ih-shud”] compares the self at death to a caterpillar that reaches the end of one blade of grass and draws itself onto the next. Hindus call the endless cycle that this idea describes samsara [“sum-SAH-ruh”], and escape from that cycle moksha.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that the eternal self, or atman, passes into a new body after death.

tossups.p: In the _Questions of King Milinda_, the monk Nagasena [“NAH-guh-SAY-nuh”] compares this process to lighting one lamp from another, since Buddhists teach that no permanent self passes from one life to the next. Buddhists picture six realms where beings may enter a new life, from gods to hell beings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that, after death, a being returns to life in a new body.

tossups.p: Tibetan Buddhists read the _Bardo Thodol_ [“BAR-doh TOH-dul”] aloud to guide a person who has died through the in-between state, lasting up to 49 days, that comes before this event. That text, often called the _Tibetan Book of the Dead_, aims to help the person reach liberation or a better new life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which, Buddhists believe, a being is born into a new life after death.

tossups.p: In 1937, a search party guided by a regent’s vision in a sacred lake found a two-year-old boy in northeastern Tibet who is said to have picked out belongings of the thirteenth Dalai Lama. Tibetan Buddhists believe that boy, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, was his predecessor returned through this process.
tossups.r: Lamas recognized this way are called tulkus. For 10 points, name this belief that a being returns in a new body after death.

tossups.p: According to the poet Xenophanes [“zeh-NOF-uh-neez”], one Greek thinker who taught this idea stopped a man from hitting a puppy because he recognized the voice of a dead friend in its cries. That thinker’s followers, the Pythagoreans [“puh-thag-uh-REE-unz”], were also famous for refusing to eat beans.
tossups.r: That thinker, Pythagoras, is also known for a theorem about right triangles. For 10 points, name this belief that souls move into new bodies after death.

tossups.p: The Greek philosopher Empedocles [“em-PED-uh-kleez”] claimed that, through this process, he had once been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird, and a fish. That thinker is better known for teaching that everything is made of four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.
tossups.r: Orphic and Pythagorean teachers held this belief too. For 10 points, name this idea that the soul passes into a new body after death.

tossups.p: In a myth that ends Plato’s _Republic_, a soldier named Er [“AIR”] revives on his funeral pyre and describes souls choosing new lives before undergoing this process, as Odysseus picks the quiet life of an ordinary man. The souls then drink from a river that makes them forget their past.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that the soul is born into a new body after death.

tossups.p: In Book Six of Virgil’s _Aeneid_ [“uh-NEE-id”], Anchises [“an-KY-seez”] shows his son crowds of souls drinking from the river Lethe [“LEE-thee”] to forget their past before this process begins. Among those waiting souls are great Romans of the future, such as Romulus and Julius Caesar.
tossups.r: Plato’s Myth of Er also describes souls drinking from such a river. For 10 points, name this belief that souls pass into new bodies after death.

tossups.p: Members of the Druze [“DROOZ”] faith believe in an immediate form of this process, in which a soul passes into a newborn human body at the very moment of death. The Druze community lives mainly in Lebanon, Syria, Israel, and Jordan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, central to Hinduism and Buddhism, that a being returns in a new body after death.

tossups.p: Followers of the mystic Isaac Luria [“LOOR-ee-uh”] described in detail a form of this idea called gilgul [“GIL-gool”], meaning “cycle” or “rolling,” in which a soul may return to finish its work in the world. Gilgul is part of Kabbalah [“kuh-BAH-luh”], Judaism’s mystical tradition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, also found in Hinduism and Buddhism, that a soul is born into a new body after death.

tossups.p: Julius Caesar wrote that the druids of Gaul taught this idea, which he believed made Gallic warriors fearless in battle. Among the Yoruba [“YOR-uh-buh”] of West Africa, names like Babatunde [“bah-bah-TOON-day”], meaning “father has returned,” reflect a form of this belief.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that a person’s soul comes back in a new body after death.

tossups.p: Sikh and Hindu tradition says that a soul may pass through 8.4 million kinds of life before it gains the rare chance of a human birth. Jains teach that through this process a soul can enter four destinies: heavenly beings, humans, animals and plants, or beings in hell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, driven by karma, that the soul returns in a new body after death.

tossups.p: In James Joyce’s _Ulysses_, Molly Bloom asks her husband what a long Greek word for this idea means, and he later recalls that she called it “met him pike hoses.” That Greek word is often used for the teachings of Pythagoras.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that souls are born into new bodies after death.

tossups.p: On the night of his enlightenment, the Buddha is said to have remembered many of his own past lives, and the Jataka [“JAH-tuh-kuh”] tales tell of those earlier lives as animals and people. Buddhists believe a person who reaches nirvana escapes this process forever.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this idea that after death a being comes back to life in a new body.

trap.title: Not karma, not resurrection
trap.body: Reincarnation tossups are full of neighboring ideas. Karma is the force of a person’s actions that shapes the next life, samsara is the whole cycle of birth and death, and moksha or nirvana is the escape from it. Resurrection, the raising of the dead taught in Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, is a different idea, and so is incarnation, a god taking bodily form, as with Vishnu’s avatars.
trap.fix: If the question describes a soul or self returning in a new body, say reincarnation; rebirth, transmigration of souls, and metempsychosis are accepted. “This force of actions” means karma, “this cycle” means samsara, and “this liberation” means moksha or nirvana.
trap.line: Real answer line: reincarnation (accept rebirth, transmigration of souls, or metempsychosis; do not accept “samsara,” “karma,” “resurrection,” or “nirvana”)
